ai.definition: AI agents are autonomous software entities designed to operate within specific or diverse environments, performing tasks with minimal human intervention.
ai.howItWorks: These agents leverage advanced machine learning algorithms to gather data from their surroundings and adapt their behavior based on the feedback they receive. This process involves continuous learning through reinforcement learning, supervised learning, and other machine learning techniques.
ai.problemSolved: AI agents address the need for efficient task execution in environments where human presence is impractical or undesirable, such as manufacturing floors, space exploration, and remote monitoring systems.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing of AI agents primarily involves developing robust software frameworks and integrating them with hardware platforms. This includes designing algorithms that can handle complex decision-making processes and ensuring the software can operate reliably in various conditions.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with defining the agent's goals, followed by selecting appropriate machine learning models, training these models on relevant datasets, testing their performance, and finally deploying them into operational environments. Continuous monitoring and updates are necessary to maintain optimal performance.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the complexity of the algorithms, the quality and quantity of data required for training, hardware requirements, and ongoing maintenance costs associated with software updates and bug fixes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook suggests steady growth as more industries recognize the benefits of AI agents in enhancing operational efficiency and reducing human error. However, challenges such as data privacy concerns and ethical considerations may limit widespread adoption.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally focus on ensuring transparency, accountability, and compliance with data protection laws. There is ongoing debate about how to regulate AI agents to prevent misuse while promoting innovation.
ai.risks: Risks include potential job displacement due to automation, cybersecurity threats, and the ethical implications of decision-making processes that may lack human oversight.
ai.profitability: Profitability depends on the specific application and market segment. Industries with high operational costs or safety risks can see significant cost savings from AI agents, making them a profitable investment.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving the generalizability of AI agents across different domains, enhancing their ability to handle complex tasks, and ensuring they operate ethically and transparently.

glossary.def: A subset of artificial intelligence that involves training algorithms to make predictions or decisions based on data.
A type of machine learning where an agent learns to behave in an environment by performing actions and receiving rewards or penalties.
A machine learning technique where the model is trained on labeled data, meaning each training example includes both input and output values.

subsystems.name: Perception
subsystems.role: turns raw sensor data into a usable picture of the world.

subsystems.name: State estimation and world model
subsystems.role: tracks where the agent and everything around it is, and predicts what happens next.

subsystems.name: Planning and decision-making
subsystems.role: chooses a route and a sequence of safe actions.

subsystems.name: Control
subsystems.role: executes the planned actions through motors, steering or other actuators.

subsystems.name: Learning and training pipeline
subsystems.role: improves the agent from data and simulation.

subsystems.name: Safety and verification
subsystems.role: keeps the agent within safe limits and detects failures.

buildSteps.title: Define the operational design domain
buildSteps.detail: Specify exactly where and when the agent must work — weather, road types, speed limits, or warehouse layout — because autonomy is only as good as its boundaries.

buildSteps.title: Build a data and simulation pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Collect sensor data from test vehicles or robots, and build a high-fidelity simulator that can generate rare and dangerous scenarios on demand.

buildSteps.title: Train perception and prediction models
buildSteps.detail: Use labelled real data and simulated data to teach the agent to recognise objects, lane markings or obstacles, and to forecast how other actors will move.

buildSteps.title: Develop the planning and control stack
buildSteps.detail: Write software that turns a goal into a safe trajectory, then into steering, throttle, brake or joint commands that hardware can follow.

buildSteps.title: Integrate on a test platform
buildSteps.detail: Mount sensors, computers and actuators on a vehicle or robot, and make all subsystems exchange data in real time without delays.

buildSteps.title: Validate in simulation and on a closed course
buildSteps.detail: Run millions of simulated kilometres and controlled track tests, hunting for edge cases that could cause a failure.

buildSteps.title: Deploy with safety monitors
buildSteps.detail: Start with a human safety driver or remote operator, and add runtime monitors that can override or stop the agent if it leaves safe limits.

buildSteps.title: Field testing and limited operation
buildSteps.detail: Operate in geofenced areas, gather data on real-world performance, and gradually reduce human supervision as reliability is proven.

buildSteps.title: Continuous improvement
buildSteps.detail: Push over-the-air updates, retrain models on newly collected data, and expand the operating domain step by step.

prerequisites.why: these are the core algorithms for perception, prediction and decision-making.
the agent needs reliable eyes and ears in rain, glare, darkness and dust.
inference must run in milliseconds on board, not in a distant data centre.
simulators speed up training enormously, but still struggle to reproduce the full complexity of the real world.
we lack proven methods to guarantee that a learned system will never cause harm in untested situations.
rules for liability and for when an agent may operate without a human are still being written.

pathway.milestone: drivers' assistance and warehouse robots work in structured settings
pathway.unlocks: safer, more efficient operations under close human oversight.

pathway.milestone: geofenced robotaxis and delivery robots operate without a safety driver in some cities
pathway.unlocks: commercial autonomous mobility in selected, well-mapped areas.

pathway.milestone: general-purpose robots learn new tasks from simulation and a few demonstrations
pathway.unlocks: flexible automation in warehouses, farms, labs and homes.

pathway.milestone: autonomous agents coordinate safely in open, unpredictable environments
pathway.unlocks: large-scale safety and productivity gains, provided verification and regulation catch up.
